summary: This Oxford University Department of Physics research page describes the Geophysical and Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics group, which studies fluid flows from garden-scale vortices to stellar, planetary and galactic phenomena. The group uses mathematical theory, numerical simulation and laboratory experiments. Its focus includes rotating and/or stratified flows, where dynamical similarity lets small rotating tanks reproduce planetary weather systems such as baroclinic cyclones and anticyclones. The page text is otherwise navigation and footer boilerplate.
one_line: Oxford Physics group studying geophysical and astrophysical fluid dynamics via theory, simulation and laboratory experiments, including rotating and stratified flows.
key_facts: The Geophysical and Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics group is a research group and research theme within the University of Oxford Department of Physics.
The group is part of the Atmospheric, Oceanic and Planetary Physics sub department.
Fluid dynamics underpins understanding of phenomena ranging from small dusty vortices generated by wind in a garden to convection in stars and planets.
The group's research embraces mathematical theory, numerical simulations and laboratory experiments.
The atmospheres, oceans and fluid interiors of any planet are described as special examples of rotating fluid systems, with or without density stratification.
Motions in planetary fluids are generated by buoyancy, surface stresses and other forces.

The group seeks to understand fundamental principles governing the dynamics, wave formation and instabilities of rotating fluids subject to mechanical stirring or shearing, differential heating and cooling, or other forces.

The laboratory work makes extensive use of dynamical similarity, where size, rotation rate or density contrast are chosen to give essentially the same balance of forces on a laboratory scale as on a planetary scale.
Using dynamical similarity, the group reproduces baroclinic cyclone and anticyclone weather systems in a rotating tank only 20-50 cm across.
Insights from laboratory experiments are applied to phenomena observed in the atmospheres or oceans of Earth or other planets.
The page lists the Clarendon Laboratory, Parks Road, Oxford, OX1 3PU as the group's location.
The group's sub-pages include About, People, Publications and Tutorials in Geophysical Fluid Dynamics.
